name: The Shadow Archives
lesson: Credential theft signs: which processes open LSASS, what access rights they ask for, dump files on disk, and whose credentials were exposed.
pivot_tip: Pivot on granted_access. Defender and svchost ask LSASS for 0x1000; something asking for 0x1FFFFF on a workstation wants to read its memory.
reaction: The dump file vanished from disk. VELVET LOCUST is cleaning up after itself.

e401.title: Sysmon 10: process access to lsass.exe
e401.tip: comsvcs.dll in the call trace plus full access to LSASS is a known way to dump credentials with built-in Windows files.

e402.title: Sysmon 11: lsass.dmp written
lines: Note: Sysmon archived a copy. The file was exfiltrated before deletion (see proxy, 09:40).
e402.tip: A ~50 MB file named like LSASS appearing in a staging folder, then deleted, means it was taken off the box.

e403.title: Ticket #48190: printer fix on WS-FIN-0142
lines: Reporter : Mira Okafor     Assignee: Tom Brooks (IT, t.brooks)
"Logged in locally on WS-FIN-0142 with my admin account to reinstall the
t.brooks groups: Domain Users, IT-Admins, Server Operators, Backup Operators
e403.tip: When an admin logs in interactively, Windows can keep their credential material in LSASS. One printer fix exposed an admin account.

e404.title: Hardening status: finance workstations
lines: ASR: Block credential stealing (LSASS) Audit      Block
Tiered admin model (no T0/T1 on WS)   No         Yes
Change ticket CHG-2231 'Enable LSA Protection': postponed (printer driver issue)
e404.tip: LSA Protection stops non-protected processes from opening LSASS. It was postponed, ironically for a printer driver.

rows.name: rundll32.exe
rows.cmdline: rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 712 C:\ProgramData\HalcyonSvc\lsass.dmp full   [inert log text]

objectives.title: Check the Sysmon pipeline
objectives.desc: Investigate SYSMON-COL for anything touching LSASS.
hints: The Sysmon Collector node is in this zone.
Press E at SYSMON-COL.
Open 'Sysmon 10: process access to lsass.exe'.

objectives.title: Who opened LSASS with full access?
objectives.desc: Hunt the access table on WS-FIN-0142 for LSASS access with anything other than the normal 0x1000.
objectives.solution: search access where target="lsass.exe" and host="WS-FIN-0142" and granted_access!="0x1000"
objectives.success: rundll32.exe with 0x1FFFFF. That's a memory read, not a health check.
hints: Lots of legitimate tools touch LSASS. The access rights are what differ.
Filter on target, host, and granted_access != "0x1000".
search access where target="lsass.exe" and host="WS-FIN-0142" and granted_access!="0x1000"

objectives.title: How was it launched?
objectives.desc: Find the rundll32.exe command line that loaded comsvcs.dll.
objectives.success: MiniDump of pid 712 (LSASS) to ProgramData. Living off the land.
hints: The call trace in e401 named a DLL.
Search the command line for that DLL name with ~.
search proc where cmdline~"comsvcs"

objectives.title: Find the dump file
objectives.desc: Hunt the file table for memory dump files.
objectives.success: lsass.dmp, 51 MB, in the same staging folder as updchk.exe.
hints: Memory dumps usually end in a particular extension.
path contains ".dmp".
search file where path~".dmp"

objectives.title: Whose secrets were in there?
objectives.desc: Collect the archived dump record, the helpdesk history, and the hardening records.
hints: Three nodes: WS-FIN-0142, HELPDESK-Q, CONFIG-DB.
Press E at each one.
Open the Sysmon 11 record, ticket #48190, and the hardening status.

objectives.title: Which other accounts logged on here?
objectives.desc: Find logons on WS-FIN-0142 by anyone other than Mira.
objectives.solution: search auth where host="WS-FIN-0142" and account!="m.okafor"
objectives.success: t.brooks logged in interactively yesterday. An IT admin's credentials were in that dump.
hints: Exclude the workstation's normal user with !=.
host is WS-FIN-0142, account is not m.okafor.
search auth where host="WS-FIN-0142" and account!="m.okafor"

objectives.title: Form a hypothesis
objectives.desc: Press B. Pin the proof and choose.
objectives.prompt: What happened in the Shadow Archives?

options.text: Defender scanned LSASS as part of a routine check
options.feedback: Defender is MsMpEng.exe asking for 0x1000. This was rundll32 asking for everything.

options.text: The adversary dumped LSASS memory with comsvcs.dll and stole credentials, including IT admin t.brooks's
Mira's password was guessed by brute force
options.feedback: No failed-logon storm here. The secrets came out of memory.
A crash doesn't write a 50 MB dump to the malware's folder and ship it out.

objectives.success: Confirmed: OS Credential Dumping from LSASS memory.
hints: Pin the LSASS access event and the helpdesk ticket.
Who opened LSASS, and whose credentials were cached?
Pin e401 and e403, then choose the comsvcs.dll option.

objectives.title: Detect it next time
objectives.prompt: Which detection would most reliably catch this behavior in future, even with a different tool?

options.feedback: rundll32 is a legitimate Windows file. Blocking its hash breaks Windows; attackers would just use another tool.

options.text: Alert on any file larger than 40 MB
options.feedback: Very noisy, and a renamed or compressed dump slips through.

options.text: Alert when a process not on an allowlist opens lsass.exe with memory-read rights (e.g. 0x1010, 0x1FFFFF)

options.feedback: Useful, but that's the C2, not credential dumping. Tools change; the behavior doesn't.

objectives.success: Exactly: detect the behavior, high on the Pyramid of Pain.
hints: Think back to the Pyramid of Pain.
Hashes and domains are easy to change. What must any dumper do?
The behavior-based LSASS access alert.

objectives.title: Map it to ATT&CK
objectives.desc: Press M and map the finding.
hints: The adversary was after secrets.
Credential Access column.
T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory.

objectives.title: Respond
objectives.desc: Press R. Preserve, then cut off what the stolen credentials can do and harden.
hints: Preserve the archived dump record before cleanup.
Reset what was exposed and stop it from happening again.
Preserve, reset t.brooks and m.okafor, enable LSA Protection, add the LSASS-access alert.

f1.text: rundll32.exe loaded comsvcs.dll and wrote LSASS memory to lsass.dmp
f1.hint: They wanted passwords and tickets from memory.

responses.label: Preserve the archived dump record and Sysmon events
responses.description: Copy the Sysmon archive and event logs to the evidence store with hashes.
responses.tradeoff: Quick. Proves exactly which credentials were exposed.
responses.feedback: Preserved. The dump record proves t.brooks and m.okafor were exposed.

responses.label: Reset t.brooks and m.okafor passwords and revoke their sessions
responses.description: Force new passwords, purge Kerberos tickets, revoke tokens.
responses.tradeoff: Brief disruption for two users. Stolen secrets stop working.
responses.too_early: Preserve the evidence first so you can prove what was exposed.
responses.feedback: Both credentials reset. The stolen copies are now stale.

responses.label: Enable LSA Protection and Credential Guard on finance workstations
responses.tradeoff: One printer driver needs an update. Worth it.
responses.feedback: LSA Protection is on. comsvcs MiniDump will fail on protected hosts.

responses.label: Deploy an alert for non-allowlisted processes opening LSASS
responses.description: Behavioral detection in EDR and Sysmon.
responses.tradeoff: Some tuning needed for security tools.
responses.feedback: Detection live. Any future dumper trips it.

responses.label: Ban IT from interactive logons on workstations (use LAPS + remote tools)
responses.tradeoff: Changes how IT works. Prevents the next printer-fix exposure.
responses.feedback: Policy approved. Admin credentials stay off workstations.

responses.label: Disable every IT admin account company-wide
responses.description: Lock out the whole IT team.
responses.tradeoff: Nobody can respond to the incident.
responses.feedback: You just locked out the people helping you contain this. Only t.brooks was exposed.

responses.label: Isolate WS-FIN-0142 now
responses.tradeoff: The stolen credentials work from anywhere. You'd only alert them.
responses.feedback: The credentials already left this box. Isolating it now just tells VELVET LOCUST you're close, while they log in somewhere else.

puzzle.title: CTF Cache: Shadow Archives
puzzle.clue: XOR with the key 0x2a. Try: decode xor cache 0x2a
